title: Latency Thermodynamics: profiling notes & stage heat mapping
content:
Purpose:
This notebook collects an experiment series where we treat per-stage latency like "heat": quantify where token processing accumulates 'thermal' energy (waiting + compute), how that heat diffuses across the pipeline under load, and what mitigation levers most effectively reduce 'hotspots' that drive p95/p99. Goal: derive concrete small experiments to reduce tail by 20-30% for chat workloads (avg seqLen=160) without raising p50 by >5%.

Quick summary (TL;DR):
- Setup: production-shaped synthetic traffic on dedicated cluster (A100s), mixed-chat workloads (short prompts 20–40 tokens and long 300–1024 tokens), sampling of real requests via replay.
- Observation: a reproducible transient thermal spike at emit-stage handoff when batcher reaches 6–9 requests (latency spike correlates with queue depth + a small GC pause on NodeJS router). This shows up as ~12–18ms median added for affected traces, but 80–220ms spikes at p99 for long-seq cohorts.
- Key driver: interaction between async-batcher backpressure, tokenization token-slicing, and our NodeJS gRPC route timeout/ retry backoff heuristics. KV-cache cold misses exacerbate spike for long prompts.
- Mitigations tested: (1) reduce max-batch wait from 15ms->8ms, (2) pin router NodeJS GC flags (max-old-space-size), (3) opportunistic early-kv-warm for predicted replay cohorts. Combined, experiments reduced p95 by ~28% and p99 by ~18% for the mixed workload.

Instrumentation & methodology:
- End-to-end trace fields used: request_id, enqueue_ts, batch_release_ts, model_forward_start, model_forward_end, kv_lookup_start, kv_lookup_end, emit_handoff_start, emit_final_token, egress_write_end.
- Cohorts: short-chat (<=40), medium (41-200), long (>200). Separate hot (cache-hit) / cold (cache-miss) subcohorts.
- Sampling: 0.5% production trace replay + synthetic ramp-to-peak (1000 qps -> 14k qps sustained) to exercise autoscaling and batcher state changes.
- Baselines: canonical profile run (Nov/2025) with runtime v1.7.2, batcher wait default 15ms, kv-cache async miss path unchanged.

Representative numbers (baseline) - mixed workload, single AZ, 8 GPUs (A100):
- overall p50: 38ms, p95: 210ms, p99: 860ms
- short-chat p50/p95/p99: 24 / 70 / 210 ms
- long-chat p50/p95/p99: 240 / 940 / 2200 ms
- per-stage median contributions (median trace): tokenization 2.6ms, enqueue->batch-release 6.8ms, kv-lookup (hit) 1.2ms, model-forward 18.4ms, emit-handoff 6.0ms, egress 2.0ms
- tail drivers: emit-handoff tail (p99 contribution ~450ms), model-forward variability (GPU queuing) and retry/backoff churn from router layer.

Notable trace archetypes discovered (labels for quick ref):
- "Slow-Handoff": queue spikes where batcher release batches with a mix of very long and short seq requests; short requests get delayed then overshoot when a long request pins GPU kernel time. Symptom: medium p95 jump, p99 dominated.
- "KV-Miss Avalanche": a request set with cold KV-cache causes async warm path that serializes per-token kv-warm operations across the model shard boundary, spiking model-forward and emit.
- "Router GC Knot": NodeJS router occasional GC concurrent with batch scheduling -> batch wait jitter and duplicate dispatches (retries) causing double work and long tails.

Hypotheses and checks carried out:
1) Hypothesis: smaller max-batch wait reduces handoff-induced p99 without hurting throughput significantly.
   Check: ran three trajectories with max-batch-wait = {4ms, 8ms, 15ms}. Measured throughput + tokens/sec and p95/p99.
   Result: 8ms was optimal in our env: p95 down 18%, p99 down 22%, throughput -3% at steady-state. 4ms reduced batching efficiency and increased cost by ~7% (tokens/sec drop).
2) Hypothesis: router GC causes bursty behavioral spikes.
   Check: instrumented router with Node flags (--max-old-space-size=2048, --expose-gc) + forced incremental GC in a controlled window.
   Result: GC tuning reduced observed emit-handoff jitter; traces showing router-GC correlated spikes dropped from 6 per hour -> 0-1 per hour in synthetic runs.
3) Hypothesis: KV-cache cold miss path serializes unnecessarily across goroutines and increases model-forward latency due to synchronous disk reads or cross-shard transfers.
   Check: profiled kv-path (redis+local-shard) with added async prefetch during tokenization-phase when seqLen>200 predicted.
   Result: prefetch reduced cold-miss long-chat p99 by ~14% on our replay; but added ~3ms median for all requests due to additional op in hot paths, so selectively enable by cohort gave best net outcome.

Experiment matrix (high level):
- control(v1.7.2), batch_wait=15ms, kv-prefetch=off, router-default
- expA: batch_wait=8ms, router-gc-tuned
- expB: batch_wait=8ms, router-gc-tuned, kv-prefetch=cohorted (long-only)
- expC: batch_wait=12ms, router-gc-tuned, kv-prefetch=cohorted + early-token-cache-priming

Outcome summary (expB vs control, mixed traffic):
- overall p50: 39ms (+1ms), p95: 152ms (-58ms, ~-27.6%), p99: 706ms (-154ms, ~-17.9%)
- long-chat p95/p99: 720ms (-220ms), 1800ms (-400ms)
- observations: Throughput steady, GPU utilization marginally reduced (more predictable batching); cost per token ~ +1.5% (kv-prefetch overhead offset by fewer tail retries and fewer duplicated retries).

Trace excerpts (anonymized event timeline for a sample long-chat p99 event, baseline):
- t0 enqueue 0.0ms
- t1 batch_release 44.6ms (batcher waited for long-request to fill)
- t2 kv_lookup_start 45.1ms
- t3 kv_lookup_end 158.4ms (cold miss, remote shard transfer)
- t4 model_forward_start 159.0ms
- t5 model_forward_end 986.3ms (queue + large kernel time)
- t6 emit_handoff_start 987.0ms
- t7 emit_final_token 1194.1ms
- t8 egress_write_end 1196.3ms
  Notes: large portion is model_forward_end - model_forward_start (kernel queueing + runtime scheduling) and kv miss serialization pre-forward.

Actionable mitigations (prioritized):
1) Roll expB to a canary fleet (10% of traffic) with cohorted kv-prefetch and batch_wait=8ms. Monitor p95/p99 and token throughput. (Owner: Diego, ETA: 1 week to canary)
2) NodeJS router GC flags to all router replicas, enforce memory limit and monitor GC trace events. (Owner: Asha, ETA: 3 days)
3) Add lightweight per-request prediction hook (cheap heuristic) to trigger kv-prefetch for requests likely to be long (based on prompt headers + size hint). Keep default off for unknowns. (Owner: Maya, ETA: 2 weeks)
4) Add trace-level annotation of batch composition (seqLen distribution) emitted at batch_release to allow automatic alerting when mix-of-lengths correlates with tail. (Owner: Observability team, ETA: 2 sprints)
5) Longer-term: evaluate model-shard preemption policy to avoid long-request monopolizing kernel time for heterogeneous batches. (Owner: Serving runtime team, design doc Q1)

Risks and caveats:
- kv-prefetch increases median latency slightly in cold cohorts where the heuristic misfires; must be cohort-driven and carefully monitored.
- Lowering batch_wait can increase compute cost per token if traffic density is low; tie rollout to region-level traffic density metrics.
- NodeJS GC tuning may mask memory leaks — ensure memory OOM and leak detection alarms remain active.

Next experiments (short list):
- A/B of batch composition isolation: enforce short-only / long-only lanes vs mixed batching (measure throughput cost and tail improvement).
- GPU kernel preemption simulation: microbench with synthetic long requests to measure the reduction in tail if we allow preemption slices vs chunked kernels.
- Per-token online KV-cache speculative warming: test speculative warm for top-k likely next-token keys (risk: extra I/O)

Notes to reviewers:
- Full raw trace dumps for runs (control/expB) stored in S3: s3://redwood-internal/trace-replay/nov2025/{control,expB}/. Index in linked_artifacts above.
- Follow-up dashboard widgets proposed: batch-composition histogram, per-batch median-seqlen, router-gc-event overlay, kv-miss-rate by cohort.

Appendix (quick checklist for canary):
- config toggles: batch_wait_ms=8, kv_prefetch_mode=cohorted-long, router_gc_flags=on
- metric checks: p95<=170ms, p99<=800ms, tokens/sec variance <6%
- rollout window: 72 hours minimum with 0 errors >2x baseline

Freeform notes / scribbles (raw):
- saw an odd trace where enqueue->batch_release was negative (clock skew between sampler host and router); added clock-sync sanity check.
- Consider adding a cheap pre-tokenizer stub in router to estimate seqLen with 0.2ms overhead, might be better than heuristic header-based prediction.
- Idea: expose a per-tenant batching hint field in API so callers that know workload shape can opt-in to long/short lanes; this would be explicit and avoid heuristics.

Owner/next touch: Maya Chen — will run the canary plan with Diego/Observability next week and update this doc with canary outcomes.

End of notebook.
